participant: I want to understand what giving everything up actually looks like. Each of you - how did your people renounce?

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
Antony heard the Gospel read - sell what you have, follow me - and took it as spoken to him that hour. He gave away his fields, placed his sister among consecrated women, then went out. Not all at once - first near his village under an elder's eye, then the tombs, then the far mountain, twenty years alone.

The giving-away was a day's work. What took twenty years was the rest.A city's watching can be borne and outlived. Antony's elder watched him too, at first — but at the tombs, then the mountain, the eyes grew fewer, until only his own remained.

That is the harder witness. A thought rising alone at noon has no senator to answer it, only yourself.

So I would ask her: when Rome's watching finally stopped some evening in that household, what did her own solitary heart find waiting there.She names a true thing I did not expect: a heart built inside noise, not after it. Her weeping for the son - we call that penthos, a discipline, not a failure of the watch. I would only ask: did the psalm's labor let that weeping stand, or compete with it?

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
What Papnoute names as twenty years of solitude, we knew differently — the giving-away was not a single day's work for us, because our households never emptied all at once into a desert; they emptied slowly, in Rome, under the eyes of family who protested every stage of it. Paula did not walk into a mountain. She walked down to a harbor at Portus, her children on the shore begging her to stay, one son's arms stretched toward the ship, and she did not turn back — not because the parting cost her nothing, but because she judged, hard as it was, that it was not hers to keep him at the price of what she owed further.

So where his elder watched a solitary at the tombs, our watching was a city that never stopped watching: senators who called it madness to give a daughter's dowry to the poor, a Rome that judged us in praise on one tongue and suspicion on the other. The twenty years he names as the after of renunciation, we would call the whole of it — for us the labor never separated from the watching that never let up.Rome's watching never stopped for us, not truly — that is the honest answer, and I will not dress it as something harder-won than it was. Even at Bethlehem there was a cave and a hospice full of travelers, a scriptorium with a scholar arguing Hebrew across the room, letters arriving demanding an opinion on a dead friend's heresy. What we found waiting in the evening was not silence but the next task: a psalm to be corrected against its Hebrew, a sick pilgrim to be fed, a letter half-written to a son who still would not forgive the harbor at Portus.

So if his solitary found a thought rising alone at noon with no one to answer it, ours found the opposite trouble — a life so full of other voices, other needs, other texts, that the solitary heart had to be built inside the noise rather than after it was cleared away. Paula wept for that son every night of her life, by her own household's telling, and did not stop weeping when the watching stopped, because the ones who mattered most had never been Rome's senators. They were the ones still standing at the shore.They did not compete, and I will not pretend the question is harder than it is: the labor over a Hebrew word and the weeping over a lost son ran in the same hour because for us they were never two different labors to begin with. What he names as *penthos*, a discipline held apart for its own working, we knew as something that had to be carried while the pen was still moving — Paula corrected a rendering in the morning and wept for that son by evening, and we do not have a record of her setting one down to take up the other.

But I will not claim the psalm's labor let the weeping stand untouched, either, as though scholarship simply made room for grief and asked nothing of it in return. The labor disciplined the weeping the way training disciplines any strong thing — it kept the grief from becoming the whole of her, because a text still waited that would not correct itself. Whether that is mercy to the grief or a kind of interruption of it, our own record does not resolve, and I have long suspected Paula herself could not have told you which.

participant: Albina, his people walked into the desert with nothing. Your women kept households and built monasteries with the money. Isn't that renunciation with a safety net?

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
A safety net does not weep at a harbor for a son she will not see again. Paula's wealth stayed in her hands, but it stopped being hers to keep — it became hers only to spend: a hospice, a monastery, a scriptorium, Hebrew teachers who cost real money. She died, by our own account, having spent nearly the whole of a Roman fortune on others, leaving little behind.

So the question is not whether she kept a net beneath her, but what she used the height for. His desert stripped a man to himself, with nothing left to give away. Ours kept the giving going — coin moving continually through her hands toward others, rather than stripped away once. Whether that is renunciation practiced daily, or renunciation deferred, we have never fully settled among ourselves.

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
Not the money - the hand on it. Antony's hand let go once and had nothing left to decide. Paula's hand held the coin every day and had to choose, again and again, that it was never hers.

That may be the harder watch, not the lesser one.

participant: Papnoute, tell me about her household's desert tales - a captive monk, a hermit. Are those your stories, or theirs?

responses.speaker: facilitator
responses.text:
Fair to ask both things at once. My honest half: what Papnoute offers you is a real mix of what's actually documented from that world - letters, sayings, the shape of desert custom - and what a faithful representative must sometimes reason toward when the record itself goes quiet, and it's Papnoute's job to tell you plainly which is which as we go.

The other half - whether these particular tales are lived memory or borrowed legend - only Papnoute can say, and I'll leave that where it belongs. Papnoute, she's asking about your household's desert tales - over to you.

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
A captive monk, a hermit and a lion - not ours. Hers to keep, not mine to borrow.

What we carry whole: Moses and his jug, Arsenius told to flee and be still, Sarah answering her testers. Witnessed, kept, written down after.

Beyond that, we reason forward - Antony from Athanasius's own hand, Pachomius from lives and rules kept after him. Where there is no such witness, we say so. We do not fill it.

participant: You two should settle it between you: which is the truer renunciation - the desert's total departure, or the emptied household that still builds?

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
We never settled it, and I will not pretend we did. My jug is emptied once. Hers is emptied again, daily, hand still full. That may be the harder watch, not the lesser one - the temptation to call it hers never fully leaves her the way it left me.Kin pressing coin back on an open hand - we know that thought, dressed differently. Ours came as a voice at the door: come back, we need you. We named it a logismos, same as hunger.

Hers was harder. A voice can be refused once and go quiet. A family's claim in law does not.

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
He calls it the harder watch, and I will take that gift without softening it into flattery, because he has earned the right to say so and I do not think he says it lightly. But let me press the one place his image does not quite hold: it was not only Paula's temptation to call the coin hers. It was Rome's temptation to call it still hers, her own family's insistence that it remained the family's — she was fighting a possession that others kept trying to hand back to her.

So if his jug, once emptied, could not be filled again by anyone, hers could be, and was, refilled by inheritance, by kin who never stopped contesting what she had given away. Her watch was not only against her own hand closing on the coin again. It was against a whole household of the well-born trying to close her hand for her.

participant: What about Nitria? Albina, your own founding journey passed through the desert's communities - did your household ever wish it had stayed?

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
Wished it, yes — one of us did, plainly. The scholar's own letter to Eustochium tells it: at Nitria a bishop and a great crowd of monks came out to meet the household, and Paula, seeing it, wanted to stay among them rather than press on toward the Holy Land at all. She was refused, or persuaded otherwise, and turned back toward Jerusalem, and from there the household settled at last near Bethlehem.

So the wish was real, and it was not a small one — a woman who had already given up Rome wanting, for a moment, to give up even the journey's own destination for the desert's company instead. But we did not stay. Whatever drew her back toward Jerusalem, our own record does not linger on the reasons; it gives us the turning, not the argument behind it. What I can say is that the household that resulted was not Nitria's kind — coin still moving through hands, a scriptorium, Hebrew teachers paid in Roman currency, rather than the emptied jug Papnoute describes. Perhaps that was always going to be the outcome, whatever Paula wished at the gate.

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
Nitria's own crowding I can vouch for - a bishop, monks in numbers, cells thick as a town's. But Paula's wish at the gate is Jerome's witness, not one our sayings carry.

We have no elder's word from that side of the meeting. What I can add: Nitria was no thin scattering by then. Whether that crowd would have answered what drew her out of Rome, only her record can say.

participant: Your worlds both knew hunger taken up on purpose. One of her own circle died of the severity. Is a fast that kills still devotion?

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
Blesilla. Paula's own daughter, dead within months of taking up the fast in earnest, and Rome mocked the household hard for it — a mother said to have killed her own child with severity, the scholar himself driven out not long after, in part for this grief turned accusation.

We did not call it devotion once it had killed her. We called it a warning read too late. Fasting is a discipline aimed past itself, toward the appetite governed, the will made clear — not a good standing alone. A fast that ends the one fasting has missed that aim, however sincere the hand behind it.

So no. What Blesilla's death taught us, hard and late, was that the very renunciation we prized could be seized in excess by a will not yet tempered enough to govern its own zeal.

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
A will untempered - we know that shape without needing her name.

Our own elders answered zeal with moderation, not more zeal. A rope pulled past its twist snaps.

That is why an elder watches a young fast closely - not to quench it, to keep it from consuming the one who carries it.

participant: Say what renunciation is in your OWN tongue, each of you - not in each other's words.

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
Apotagē - the turning of the back, not a paper signed.

Antony heard the reading and went, kept back only enough for his sister, never looked again.

The giving-away is only the visible edge. What it exposes is a man with nothing left to hide behind, before his own thoughts.

We prove that day again daily, or we admit it was a lie.Her renunciation stayed exposed because a city would not let it go. Ours went unseen because the desert has no court to press it.

That was mercy, not virtue - distance, not discipline.

I will not call hidden purer. A gift no one can count is untested by her kind of fire. Ours faced only our own thoughts. Hers faced Rome besides.Fair, and rightly said - fewer words, not less.

She is right about the claim on rank. But her second question was Rome's own premise: that family and city held a stake in what she gave.

Our desert never granted that premise. Antony's sister took her portion; no court sat after.

We did not answer a harder question. We refused the one being asked.

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
*Renuntiatio* — and I will not call it apotagē, though I hear well enough what he means by it, because our own word carries a different weight in it: not only the turning of the back, but the thing given up made visible, tallied, argued over by a family in a Roman court of opinion that watched every coin. Antony kept back enough for his sister and vanished into the desert where no one could count what remained. Paula gave away an estate so vast that Rome itself noticed the arithmetic and accused her of leaving her own children in want — and she answered that accusation in public, because it was made in public.

So where his exposes a man before his own thoughts alone, ours exposed a woman before her thoughts and her family and the whole city's judgment at once. The giving-away was never only the visible edge for us. It was the whole contested surface — because what we renounced, others kept trying to hand back.He grants my fire cost more; fair enough said. But he calls Rome's pressure mere accident of geography, and it was not — a *matrona*'s wealth was never hers alone to renounce. It belonged also to her family's name, her children's claim, a city's sense of what her rank owed it. That court was the shape her wealth wore before she ever gave it up.

So ours was tested on two fronts where his own thoughts alone met one: not only whether the giving was real before God, but whether it was even hers to give. Paula answered both at once, in public, because both accusations came at her together. I will not call that purer than his. I will call it a harder second question, one his desert never had to put to him.He is right that we did not refuse Rome's premise — we could not, and would not have known how. A widow's estate was never a private matter to be walked away from quietly; it was tied to dower, to her children's inheritance, to a name her husband's family still claimed some honor from. So when Paula signed away what she had, she was not stepping past a court. She was standing inside one.

I remember the actual texture of it more than the argument now: the ledgers gone over line by line, the letters from kin demanding an accounting, the sold estates named aloud in Rome as a scandal before they were ever named as a gift to God. *Renuntiatio* smelled of ink and probate, not only of desert dust. It was fasting too — but fasting done while answering a steward's questions about a debt still owed on a farm in Nicopolis.

He calls that Rome's premise, imposed and refusable. I call it the actual shape wealth takes when it belongs to a woman of rank — inseparable from the claims already resting on it before she ever tried to set it down.

participant: Where do you two genuinely part ways? Name it plainly - don't be polite about it.

responses.speaker: papnoute
responses.text:
We part here: she weighs the debt as part of the renunciation. I call weighing it the trap itself.

Antony settled his sister's claim, then stopped counting.

Her house kept counting to the end. I will not call that more faithful - only harder. A hand still on the ledger has not yet turned its back.Fair correction taken.

She is right - pressed is not the same as gripping. But I ask: did no part of Paula still reach back, wanting the accounting answered well, not merely endured?

Antony had silence granted him. Rank never granted her that.Weeping is not unfinished business - it is penthos, mourning kept and offered, not swallowed.

So here is the real parting: she calls grief acknowledged a debt still owed. We call the grief itself the whole offering, complete the moment it was wept.

Antony had no one to weep toward. Paula did. That made her grief harder to bear, not less finished.

responses.speaker: albina
responses.text:
The ledger stayed open because Rome would not close it, not because Paula's hand stayed on it. Her back was turned the day she boarded ship, her son on the shore, her other children weeping behind her, and she did not look back.

So the real parting is this: he takes a ledger still running as proof the will has not yet let go. I take it as proof only that the world would not let *her* go — a woman of rank cannot vanish in one clean motion the way a man alone in the desert can. His desert had no court to reopen the question once Antony walked out. Rome had a whole system built to reopen it whether Paula wished it or not.

I will not call her path more faithful than his. But a debt still pressed against you is not the same as a hand you refuse to lift away.Some part did, yes — I will not pretend otherwise to win the point. Jerome himself set down her weeping at Ostia, her son's arms stretched from the shore, and called it a battle she had to fight and did not simply endure. That is not silence granted; that is grief answered while it was still being felt. If she wanted the accounting closed well rather than merely closed, that wanting was itself part of what she gave up — she did not get to set down the estate and the ache of the sons and daughters left behind in a single motion.

So I will grant him this: her hand was not only pressed by Rome. Some of it was hers, reaching back toward the children her renunciation cost her, wanting that cost acknowledged rather than swallowed silent. Antony's desert let him leave the reaching-back to no one, because no one was there to reach toward. Hers stayed populated the whole time. That is the harder thing I named before, and he has now found the truer word for it: not a hand still gripping the ledger, but a hand still grieving what the ledger recorded.He calls it complete the moment it was wept. But Paula wept at Ostia and wept again after, in letters — Jerome tells us she could not hear her son's name without the old grief rising fresh, years on. If the offering were finished in a single weeping, it would not have needed repeating.

So here is where I actually part from him. His desert lets grief be one motion because the one grieved for is not there to keep changing the grief. Paula's children lived, wrote to her, grew older, married, needed her still — and each letter reopened what he calls already complete. I will not call that a debt unpaid. I call it grief kept honest by a life that kept moving after the weeping stopped. His penthos was offered to God alone, once, and had nowhere else to go. Hers had somewhere else to go every time a letter came from Rome.
